newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Valero refining head sees growth as key.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Valero refining head sees growth as key.

text.p: Valero Energy Corp, fresh from making a splashy deal to enter the realm of the top U.S. independent refiners, will continue looking toward further growth, its top refining executive said Tuesday.
"We're not going to rest on our laurels," Baines Manning, Valero's executive vice president for refining and marketing, told Reuters in an interview at Valero's headquarters here.
"We're not going to stop with what we've just done," Manning said, referring to the company's $485 million purchase of Basis Petroleum Inc's three U.S. Gulf Coast refineries.
The deal for Basis, Salomon Inc's refining unit, gives Valero four Gulf Coast refineries with a total of 500,000 barrels per day (bpd) of refining capacity.
Manning said Valero was not seeking any particular refining capacity level, but said growing bigger meant lowering costs and staying competitive.

"We're going to continue to grow ourselves to get ... bigger critical mass," Manning said. "And in doing so we reduce our overhead, we reduce our per-barrel operating cost, and that's the name of our game," Manning said.
He also said the time was right to be buying refineries.

"We think that the timing is good right now to buy refining assets. We feel we're at or near the bottom of the refining cycle," he said, referring to poor profit margins in recent years that he thought would get better as demand catches up to refining capacity. He did not say when Valero would buy again.
He noted that the three Basis refineries have a replacement cost of $3 billion, which means Valero paid 10 cents on the dollar for the assets.

He also said the Basis assets are relatively modern, noting Salomon spent money to upgrade certain units at the Krotz Springs, Louisiana plant and the Houston and Texas City, Texas refineries, which has spared Valero the same expensive task.

"They took the first step and there are other things we'll be taking a look at," Manning said referring to future projects planned at Texas City and Houston aimed at upgrading cracking residual fuel into lighter products like diesel or gasoline.

"With their ability to process heavy sour crudes, we're looking at what I call a double margin play. One, we think the crack spread is going to improve. And we also feel like the heavy-light (crude) differential is going to improve," he said.
Responding to a question on what many feel remains Valero's Achilles heel in the future--namely the absence of retail assets, Manning said his company does not share those concerns.
He said that while Valero has not dismissed the idea of buying retail assets in some future acquisition, the company has reservations with traditional retailing concepts.

"We feel the marketing of gasoline is a merchandising operation today. It's not a situation like we had back 15, 20, 30 years ago in which the only place you went to buy gas was at a gas station. But today you can buy gasoline at a lot of different locations."
He said that many of new retail outlets, such as "megastores", are likely to discount gasoline to attract clients to whom they then sell other more profitable items.

He said the emergence of federally mandated clean fuels in the 1990s has begun to erode the perception that non-branded gasoline is inferior in quality, and as a consequence, brand loyalty is beginning to fade.
He said retail margins, the spread between spot and pump prices, have already begun to shrink, and that over the longer term, rationalization may come to the retail sector.
"We think there could be a retail rationalization," Manning said.
-- New York Energy Desk 1 212 859 1620
